en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
8. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Hemaka:
"Those who previously gave me an explanation," [said the Venerable Hemaka].
"Alas! From the teaching of Gotama;
'It was thus,' 'it will be thus'—all that is mere hearsay."
All that is merely an increase of reasoning;
I found no delight therein.
As for those who previously explained things to me—the brahmin Bāvarī and his other teachers—they [merely] held their own views.

They explained, declared, taught, defined, established, disclosed, analyzed, clarified, and revealed their own preference, their own inclination, their own view, their own disposition, and their own intention—
those who previously explained things to me in such a manner.
"Thus said the Venerable Hemavata.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a grammatical conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...this is the sequential order of the words: "thus" (*iccā*).
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment...
[as before] ... "Hemaka" is the name of that brahmin... [as before] ... "designation"—thus it was said by the venerable Hemaka.

"Huraṁ gotamasāsanā" means: beyond the teaching of Gotama, after the teaching of Gotama, before the teaching of Gotama, earlier than the teaching of Gotama—the teaching of the Buddha, the teaching of the Conqueror, the teaching of the Tathāgata, the teaching of the Arahat—this is "huraṁ gotamasāsanā.
"Iccāsi, iti bhavissati" means: thus indeed it was, thus indeed it will be.
"It was thus," or "it will be thus"—all that is based on "thus-it-was-said" (itihītiha).

All that is based on "thus-it-was-said" is through oral tradition, succession, the handing down of the scriptures, reasons for conjecture, reasons for logic, pondering over modes, and approval resulting from reflection on views; it is not known by one's own direct higher knowledge.
"They did not speak of a dhamma that was directly verifiable by themselves"—
all that is "thus-it-was-said" (itihītiha).
"All that is an increase of reasoning"— all that is an increase of reasoning, an increase of discursive thought (vitakka), and an increase of intention (saṅkappa).
Increasing thoughts of sensual desire, increasing thoughts of ill will, increasing thoughts of cruelty, increasing thoughts of relatives, increasing thoughts of one’s native land,
increasing thoughts of immortality, increasing thoughts associated with lack of sympathy for others,
and increasing thoughts associated with gain, honor, and praise, as well as thoughts associated with not being held in contempt.
All that is merely an increase of speculative reasoning.
"I did not delight therein" means: I did not find delight therein, I did not experience it, I did not attain it, I did not obtain it—I did not delight therein.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“Those who previously explained it to me...
(Thus spoke the Venerable Hemaka.)
"Alas, from the teaching of Gotama!
'It was thus,' 'it will be thus'—
all that is merely hearsay."
"All that merely increases speculative reasoning;
I do not delight therein.
Therefore, you yourself explain the Dhamma to me."
The Sage who has eradicated craving—
having understood this and living mindfully—
crosses over the clinging in the world.
"And you, explain the Dhamma to me.
He addresses the Blessed One as "you" (*tvam*).
"Explain the Dhamma" means: [explain it].
The Dhamma: that which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; with its own meaning and its own phrasing;

entirely complete and pure; namely, the holy life (brahmacariya), the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and Nibbāna together with the way leading to Nibbāna.
"Declare the way; explain it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and manifest it—do you yourself declare the Dhamma to me.
O Sage, [teach] that which destroys craving."
Craving means craving for forms … pe … craving for mental phenomena.
The destruction of craving, the abandoning of craving, the stilling of craving, the relinquishment of craving, the subsiding of craving, is the deathless Nibbāna.
"Muni": *mona* is said to be knowledge... [as before] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a "muni"—thus, a muni is one who has destroyed craving.
"Having understood that, they live mindfully": having understood that, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having analyzed it, and having made it manifest.
Having made it known, weighed, judged, clarified, and fully understood that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and likewise that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering" ...
and likewise that "all phenomena are non-self" ... [and so on].
“Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease”—having made this known, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having analyzed it, and having made it manifest.
One is mindful by way of four reasons:
one is mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body ... [and so on].
Thus he is called "mindful.
Walking, standing, sitting, moving about, acting, protecting, maintaining, and sustaining—
one who acts while knowing this is said to be "walking mindfully."
"Entanglement in the world": "entanglement" (visattikā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
That which is lust, infatuation ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
In what sense is it "entanglement"? ... It is "entanglement" because it is spread out and extensive.
"In the world" means in the world of the lower realms, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases.

"One should cross over attachment to the world" means: attachment is a clinging in the world; one should cross over, transcend, surmount, pass beyond, and go beyond that attachment in the world—thus, "one should cross over attachment to the world."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“O Sage, you must explain to me the Dhamma that destroys craving.”
"Having understood this, one who dwells mindfully may cross over attachment to the world"—
referring here to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
O Hemaka, among things that are dear,
the dispelling of desire and lust is the deathless state of Nibbāna.
"Herein, regarding the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized":
"the seen" is what is seen with the eye;
"the heard" is what is heard with the ear.
They are smelt by the nose, tasted by the tongue, touched by the body,
and cognized by the mind as "cognized"—
this refers here to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
"Regarding 'gold among things dear,' what in the world is dear and pleasant?
The eye is dear and pleasant in the world; the ear in the world... the nose in the world... the tongue in the world... the body in the world...

the mind is dear and pleasant in the world. Visible forms are dear and pleasant in the world; sounds in the world... odors in the world... tastes in the world... tangibles in the world... mental phenomena are dear and pleasant in the world."
Eye-consciousness is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; ear-consciousness is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
nose-consciousness in the world … tongue-consciousness in the world … body-consciousness in the world … mind-consciousness is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
eye-contact in the world … ear-contact in the world … nose-contact in the world … tongue-contact in the world … [body-contact in the world … mind-contact in the world].
In the world... bodily contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world... mental contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;

feeling born of eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world... feeling born of ear-contact... feeling born of nose-contact... feeling born of tongue-contact... feeling born of body-contact... feeling born of mind-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world.

In the world, that which is pleasant and agreeable consists of the perception of forms in the world… the perception of sounds in the world… the perception of odors in the world… the perception of tastes in the world… the perception of tangibles in the world… the perception of mental phenomena in the world,
which is pleasant and agreeable; as well as volition regarding forms in the world… volition regarding sounds in the world… [and so forth].
In the world, volition regarding odors, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding tangibles, and volition regarding mental phenomena in the world is a lovely form,
a pleasant form; craving for forms in the world,

craving for sounds in the world, craving for odors in the world, craving for tastes in the world, craving for tangibles in the world, and craving for mental phenomena in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form.

In the world, thought directed toward forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; in the world, thought directed toward sounds... thought directed toward odors... thought directed toward tastes... thought directed toward tangibles... thought directed toward mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing.

In the world, sustained thought directed toward forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; in the world, sustained thought directed toward sounds... sustained thought directed toward odors... sustained thought directed toward tastes... sustained thought directed toward tangibles... sustained thought directed toward mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing—these, O Hemaka, are among the lovely things in the world.
"Dispelling lustful passion" (*chandārāgavinodana*):

"Lustful passion" (*chandārāga*) refers to that which is desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, clinging to sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, the clinging to sensual pleasures, and the hindrance of desire for sensual pleasures.
"Dispelling lustful passion" means the abandoning of lustful passion, the subsiding of lustful passion, the relinquishing of lustful passion, the stilling of lustful passion—the deathless *Nibbāna*.
The dispelling of desire and lust.
The deathless state of Nibbāna is the state of Nibbāna—the state of refuge, the state of shelter, the state of sanctuary, the state of fearlessness.
"Deathless" means permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.
The deathless state of Nibbāna.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Herein, regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized...”
“O Hemaka, among things that are dear,
the dispelling of desire and lust is the deathless state of Nibbāna.”
Having understood this, those who are mindful,
having attained extinction in this very life, are always at peace.
"Having crossed over attachment to the world—
those who are mindful, having understood this.
"This" refers to the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
"Having understood" means having understood, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest.
Having understood, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest that "all formations are impermanent."

“Having understood, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest the fact that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘all phenomena are non-self’ … and ‘whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.’”
Furthermore, the Arahants are "mindful" because their taints are exhausted.
They are mindful by virtue of four reasons:
they are mindful because they have developed the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, and so forth.
Those who are mindful are called "the mindful"—
having understood this, they are those who are mindful.
They are "extinguished in this very life."
“Seen in this very life” means seen as phenomena, known as phenomena, weighed as phenomena, deliberated upon as phenomena, manifested as phenomena,
and fully clarified as phenomena. “All conditioned formations are impermanent”—

this is seen as a phenomenon …pe… “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease”— this is seen as a phenomenon, known as a phenomenon, weighed as a phenomenon, deliberated upon as a phenomenon, manifested as a phenomenon, and fully clarified as a phenomenon.
“Completely extinguished” means: they are extinguished because greed has been extinguished; they are extinguished because hatred has been extinguished;
they are extinguished because delusion has been extinguished; [and so on] because anger... resentment...
all unwholesome volitional formations have been calmed, stilled, pacified, burnt away, extinguished, vanished, and subsided; thus they are at peace.
“Calmed, thoroughly calmed, extinguished, and tranquilized”—
thus they are “extinguished in this very life.
And they are “ever calmed.”
"Peaceful" means: because greed has been stilled and extinguished, they are peaceful; ... [and so on] ... because of hatred, delusion, anger, and resentment;

... [and so on] ... because all unwholesome volitional formations have been calmed, pacified, tranquillized, burnt away, quenched, vanished, and subsided, they are calm, peaceful, tranquil, quenched, and subsided—thus they are "peaceful."
Those Arhats are those whose taints are exhausted.
"Always" means at all times, at every time, constantly, perpetually, continuously, uninterruptedly, in immediate succession,
without interval, incessantly, and persistently— whether before a meal or after a meal, during the first watch of the night, or the middle watch.
During the middle watch and the last watch, in the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight, in the rainy season, the winter, or the summer;
in the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, or the final stage of life—
they are always at peace.
"Crossed over the clinging in the world": here "clinging" (*visattikā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
In what sense is it "clinging"? ... It is called clinging because it is spread out and extensive.
"In the world": in the world of the states of deprivation … [and so on] … in the world of the sense bases.

"Crossed over the clinging in the world": clinging is indeed in the world; having crossed over that clinging in the world—having crossed it, gone beyond it, passed over it, transcended it, and surmounted it—one is said to have "crossed over the clinging in the world."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having understood this, those who are mindful are extinguished in this very life.”
"And they are always at peace,
having crossed over the world's attachment.
At the conclusion of this verse, ...pe...
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This concludes the eighth exposition: The Questions of the Young Brahmin Hemaka.
